How is infection prevented in the audiology clinic? In this lesson we learn standard precautions, the five moments of hand hygiene, the Spaulding classification, cleaning and disinfecting equipment, single-use parts, and safety when taking ear impressions.

AIHEAR Audiology Academy makes short, clear lessons for audiology students and professionals.

Sources: World Health Organization, WHO Guidelines on Hand Hygiene in Health Care (2009); CDC, Guideline for Disinfection and Sterilization in Healthcare Facilities (2008); Siegel JD et al., CDC Guideline for Isolation Precautions (2007); ASHA, Infection Control (Practice Portal); Katz J et al. Handbook of Clinical Audiology.

This video is for educational purposes and does not replace diagnosis or treatment.

cumleler: Hello, and welcome to the AIHEAR Audiology Academy.
In this lesson we will learn about infection control, standard precautions and equipment disinfection in the audiology clinic.
We will also look at single-use parts, safety when taking ear impressions, and other safety issues in the clinic.
Infection control is the set of practices that prevent microorganisms from passing between patients, staff and the environment.
In audiology the most common route is contact; a clinician's hand can carry microorganisms to an ear, and from that ear to another patient.
Instruments used with many patients, such as earphones, probes and the response button, can spread infection through indirect contact.
Long conversations at close range can spread respiratory infections through droplets.
Contact with body fluids and secretions, such as ear discharge, blood and cerumen, needs extra precautions.
Some of our patients are babies, older adults or people with weak immunity; so the rules are applied to everyone, every time.
Standard precautions are basic rules applied the same way to every patient, whether or not an infection is known.
The most effective of these is hand hygiene: an alcohol-based hand rub, or washing with soap and water.
Gloves are worn if contact with discharge, blood or broken skin is possible; gloves do not replace hand hygiene.
All instruments that touch the patient are cleaned and disinfected after every patient, by a method the institution approves.
Used single-use parts and soiled materials go into the right bin, following the institution's waste rules.
Offering a mask to a coughing patient and reminding them to use tissues are also part of respiratory hygiene.
The World Health Organization defines five moments for hand hygiene; the first is before touching a patient.
The second is just before a clean procedure, such as taking an ear impression or placing a probe in the ear canal.
The third is after a procedure with a risk of contact with body fluids, such as discharge or blood.
The fourth is after touching the patient, when leaving the patient's side.
The fifth is after touching surfaces around the patient, such as the chair or equipment, even if you did not touch the patient.
These moments repeat many times in one audiology visit; placing hand rub inside and outside the booth makes this easier.
To decide which process an instrument needs, the Spaulding classification is widely used.
Instruments that enter sterile tissue or the bloodstream are critical and are sterilized.
Instruments that touch mucosa or broken skin are semicritical and need high-level disinfection.
Instruments that touch only intact skin are noncritical; low- or intermediate-level disinfection is enough.
Most instruments used in audiology touch intact ear canal skin, so they are noncritical.
For instruments that touch a draining or injured ear, single-use parts or a higher-level process are preferred.
Cleaning is removing visible soil, cerumen and organic matter from a surface with water, detergent and mechanical wiping.
Disinfection is reducing microorganisms on nonliving surfaces by chemical or physical means.
Sterilization is destroying all forms of microorganisms, including spores.
Because soil reduces a disinfectant's effect, cleaning always comes before disinfection.
The institution's infection control unit decides which product to use; the audiologist follows that protocol.
Parts that enter the ear canal need the most care in infection control.
The foam tips of insert earphones are single-use; a new one is fitted for each patient.
Tympanometry and otoacoustic emission probe tips are also single-use, or are cleaned by the method the manufacturer recommends.
The probe body holding the tip is also wiped after every patient; if cerumen got into the tip, the probe is checked.
A single-use otoscope speculum is thrown away; reusable specula are processed under the institution's protocol.
No part soiled with cerumen or discharge is used on the next patient without cleaning.
Insert foam tips are single-use and are thrown away after the patient.
If probe tips are not single-use, they are cleaned and disinfected by the method in the manufacturer's instructions.
Supra-aural earphone cushions are wiped with a suitable disinfectant after every patient; worn cushions are replaced.
The bone vibrator and its headband touch the skin, so they are wiped after every patient.
The response button and chair arms are high-touch surfaces that are often forgotten.
For otoscope specula, the institution's single-use or reprocessing rule is followed.

maddeler.metin: Compatible with the device maker's advice

cumleler: A disinfectant should be a product approved by the institution's infection control unit, with its effectiveness stated on the label.
Every product has a contact time stated on its label; if the surface does not stay wet for that time, the effect drops.
For earphones, probes and hearing aids, use products the device maker recommends; some chemicals damage plastics and membranes.
Liquid products are not sprayed directly on a device; they are first applied to a cloth or wipe.
Gloves are worn and the room is ventilated according to the product's safety information.
Hearing aids received from patients are also cleaned by the same rules before checks and repairs.
Taking an ear impression places material in the ear canal and is a procedure that needs care.
First, the ear canal and tympanic membrane are assessed with otoscopy, looking for cerumen, discharge, a perforation or a wound.
With a perforation, active discharge or recent ear surgery, a physician's view is sought before the impression is taken.
To keep the impression material from reaching the tympanic membrane, an otoblock of the right size is placed in the ear canal.
The otoblock is advanced carefully, using a light source, until it is past the second bend of the ear canal.
Once the material has set, the impression is removed slowly, and otoscopy is repeated to check that no material is left in the canal.
Altered anatomy, such as a mastoidectomy cavity, needs more experience; if needed, an experienced colleague is consulted.
The impression procedure begins with hand hygiene and otoscopy.
The otoblock is placed under light, with its thread left outside, without causing the patient discomfort.
The impression material is filled from deep in the ear canal outward, without leaving air bubbles.
The setting time stated by the manufacturer is observed; meanwhile, the patient does not talk or move their jaw.
After the impression is removed, otoscopy is repeated and the result, and anything unusual, is recorded.
In vestibular tests and with dizzy patients there is a fall risk; patients are supported while walking and getting off the table.
Ask about allergy to latex and some impression materials; for a patient with an allergy history, suitable materials are chosen.
Equipment calibration and electrical safety checks are done regularly; damaged cables are not used.
When fitting a high-output hearing aid, the maximum output level is carefully limited and the patient's comfort is monitored.
Before every procedure, identity is verified with two separate identifiers; a correct procedure on the wrong patient is also a safety error.

sahneler.metin: Put a hand rub dispenser inside and outside the booth, and list the surfaces to wipe after every patient on a checklist.
cumleler: A tip from the field: put an alcohol-based hand rub both inside and outside the booth.
List the surfaces to wipe after every patient on a short checklist: earphones, vibrator, probe, response button and chair arms.
Hang the list on the booth wall; on a busy day, the step most often forgotten is the response button.
Show this list to new staff and trainees on their first day.

maddeler.metin: The five moments of hand hygiene
Tips entering the ear are single-use

cumleler: Standard precautions are applied the same way to every patient; the most effective measure is hand hygiene.
Hand hygiene is done before contact, before a clean procedure, after fluid risk, after contact and after touching the surroundings.
Tips entering the ear canal are single-use or processed by the maker's method; other surfaces are wiped after every patient.
Otoscopy is done before and after an ear impression; the otoblock protects the tympanic membrane.

secenekler: A new foam tip each patient
sahneler.aciklama: Gloves _do not replace hand hygiene_; hand hygiene is also done after removing gloves.

cumleler.yazi: Test yourself: which of the following practices is not appropriate for infection control?

cumleler: The correct answer is B: skipping hand hygiene because you are wearing gloves.
Gloves can tear and hands can get soiled when removing them; so hand hygiene is done before and after gloves.
